nature-gov-132.title: A treaty against air pollution that crosses borders
nature-gov-132.text: Air pollution ignores borders, so smoke from one country can fall as acid rain on another. The Convention on Long-Range Transboundary Air Pollution, a UNECE treaty, commits its parties to limit, reduce and prevent such pollution. It opened for signature on 13 November 1979 and entered into force on 16 March 1983. It now has 51 parties. Eight protocols set specific cuts, such as the 1985 Helsinki Protocol on sulphur and the 1999 Gothenburg Protocol on acidification and ground-level ozone. It was an early effort to treat the atmosphere as a shared global resource.

nature-gov-145.title: The London Convention: no more dumping at sea
nature-gov-145.text: Ships, aircraft and platforms once dumped waste into the sea with few limits. A treaty signed on 29 December 1972 set out to control that pollution. It entered into force on 30 August 1975, using a "black list" of banned materials and a "grey list" needing special care. Its Protocol of 17 November 1996 flipped the logic to a "reverse list": any dumping not explicitly allowed is banned. The protocol also wrote in the precautionary approach and the polluter pays principle. In 2013 its parties adopted binding rules for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization. It does not cover pipes and outfalls on land.

nature-gov-136.title: The Forest Principles: a compromise on the world's forests
nature-gov-136.text: At the 1992 summit in Rio, forests split rich and poor nations. Developing countries in the Group of 77 wanted more aid to pay for forest reserves, and the final text was a compromise. The Forest Principles are non-binding recommendations for conserving and sustainably developing every kind of forest. They tied deforestation to third world debt and weak technology transfer. They said the extra cost of saving forests should be shared fairly. They led in 1994 to the Montréal Process, which set criteria and indicators for temperate and boreal forests.

nature-gov-112.title: Earth system governance: steering a planet in the Anthropocene
nature-gov-112.text: Humans now change the whole Earth system, so who steers that change? Earth system governance is the research field built around the question. In simple terms, it studies the rules and efforts of actors at every level, local to global, that aim to prevent, reduce and adapt to environmental change. Frank Biermann developed the idea in a lecture published in 2007, and the global Earth System Governance Project began in 2009. It draws on political science, sociology, economics, ecology, policy studies, geography, sustainability science and law. Its research centers on five linked problems: architecture, agency, adaptiveness, accountability and legitimacy, and allocation and access. Four themes cut across them: power, knowledge, norms and scale. Every level matters, not just the global one. Critics call the field too top-down. Mike Hulme argues it is hubristic to try to control the global climate through universal regimes. Defenders reply that this reading of the concept is too narrow.

nature-gov-123.title: Managing the coast as one system
nature-gov-123.text: Coastal margins cover 8% of the world's surface but provide 25% of global resources. About 70% of people live within a day's walk of a coast. Integrated coastal zone management tries to manage this crowded strip sustainably, across geographic and political boundaries, weighing nature, society and the economy together. It was developed at the 1992 summit in Rio and set out in Chapter 17 of Agenda 21. It runs in five steps: assess the situation, plan, embed the plan in institutions, implement, and keep evaluating. There is no end state. Its main obstacles are institutional, not technical. Because the coast is treated as common property, top-down control is hard.

nature-gov-151.title: The three Rio Conventions
nature-gov-151.text: The June 1992 summit in Rio de Janeiro, described in {{ref:nature-hist-003}}, produced three conventions, on climate, biodiversity and desertification. The UNFCCC aims to hold greenhouse gas levels where they prevent dangerous human interference with the climate. The CBD has three goals: conserve biodiversity, use it sustainably, and share fairly the benefits drawn from the genes of living things. The UNCCD ties sustainable land management to land degradation and aims for no net loss of healthy land, with a focus on restoring drylands. The summit also produced Agenda 21, the Forest Principles and the Rio Declaration.

nature-res-198.title: Polycentric governance: many centers, no single boss
nature-res-198.text: Must every shared resource be run either by a central government or by private owners? Vincent Ostrom said no. Polycentric governance means rule by many overlapping, independent decision-making centers at different scales, instead of one central authority. Ostrom argued that such systems can improve efficiency, accountability and problem-solving. The idea suggested that self-organizing systems often beat top-down solutions. His wife and colleague, Elinor, added that key management decisions should be made as close as possible to the events and people involved. The approach has limits. A resource that cannot be monitored as a whole, such as space debris, is less likely to be well managed in a polycentric network. Critics also question whether it works where institutions are weak or corruption is high.

nature-gov-138.title: Governing through goals
nature-gov-138.text: Some global governance works without binding law. In global goal-setting, countries sign up to goals that are not legally binding, keep flexibility in how they meet them, and lack strong institutions to enforce them. The UN's goals for sustainable development from 2015 to 2030 are an example. They followed the Millennium Development Goals, which ran from 2000 to 2015.

nature-gov-139.title: Orchestration: steering the world indirectly
nature-gov-139.text: An international organization often lacks the power to order anyone around. Orchestration is its workaround. It is a soft, indirect form of global steering: the organization recruits willing intermediaries, who then influence a target group. It complements existing regimes and fills their gaps through three activities: agenda setting, coordination and support. The UN's five regional economic commissions, for example, act as orchestrators for the UN's goals for sustainable development.

nature-gov-118.title: Institutional fit: matching rules to the problem's size
nature-gov-118.text: A river basin may span three countries while each country manages only its own stretch. Institutional fit is the match, or mismatch, between the scale of an environmental problem and the level at which policy tackles it. Mismatches make interventions work less well. The political economist Ostrom and others argued that mismatch often causes unsustainable management, and no simple fixes have been found. Getting agencies and communities to cooperate across scales is one attempt to close the gap.

nature-gov-146.title: Marine spatial planning: zoning the sea
nature-gov-146.text: A single stretch of sea may host fishing boats, shipping lanes, wind farms and protected habitat at once. Marine spatial planning is a public process that maps and allocates where and when human activities happen at sea, to meet goals set through politics. It works like land-use planning for marine waters, using maps of how an area is used and what habitats it holds. Planners can weigh the combined effects of maritime industries and reduce conflicts among users. The aim is to use marine resources within clear environmental limits, so ecosystems stay healthy. The EU required its coastal member states to set up plans by 2021, covering fishing, aquaculture, conservation, shipping and renewable energy. Planning can also speed offshore wind and other renewables by streamlining licensing.

nature-gov-130.title: The Basel Ban: closing the recycling loophole
nature-gov-130.text: Waste traders had found a loophole: call a shipment "recycling" and send it abroad. The original Basel Convention only required prior informed consent. The Basel Ban Amendment of 1995 bans hazardous waste exports from mostly OECD developed countries to developing countries, for any reason, recycling included. Industry groups, Australia and Canada strongly opposed it. Parties even disagreed over how many ratifications it needed. Croatia became the 97th country to ratify on 6 September 2019, and the ban entered into force on 5 December 2019.

nature-gov-144.title: The Lisbon Principles for shared resources
nature-gov-144.text: In 1997, the ecological economist Costanza set out six principles for governing the oceans and other shared resources sustainably. Access to a resource brings a duty to use it in ways that are ecologically sustainable, economically efficient and socially fair. When irreversible harm is possible but uncertain, decisions should err toward caution. The burden of proof falls on those whose activities may cause damage. All costs and benefits, including those borne by outsiders, should be counted, and markets adjusted to reflect full costs where appropriate. Governance should sit at the scale with the best information and quickest response, and every stakeholder should take part.

nature-gov-114.title: Earth system law: law for a whole planet
nature-gov-114.text: Law has usually been built around nations and property. Earth system law, a young branch of earth system governance, imagines law rooted instead in the planetary scale of the Anthropocene and its social and ecological crisis. As of 2021 the idea was still in its infancy. Its precise content, purpose and scope remain a work in progress.

nature-gov-113.title: Planetary justice: fairness for people and nature
nature-gov-113.text: One kind of justice asks whether people share environmental harms fairly. Planetary justice widens the circle. It covers fairness among people and also between people and the rest of the living world. Scholars called for it as early as 1972. Five main approaches to caring for the planet exist: market liberal, bioenvironmentalist, ecomodernist, institutionalist and social green. None yet offers a vision of justice that puts the poor first.

nature-gov-143.title: Freedom of the seas: can anyone own the ocean?
nature-gov-143.text: In 1609 Hugo Grotius argued in Mare Liberum that the sea, like the air, cannot be occupied and belongs to everyone's use. John Selden answered in Mare Clausum that states could claim the sea just like land. Grotius's view became the principle of freedom of the seas: the open sea is international territory that every nation may use and none may own. National waters long stopped at a narrow belt, usually three nautical miles, under the "cannon shot" rule. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea later replaced the old concept.

nature-gov-161.title: Sharing rivers across borders
nature-gov-161.text: Many rivers flow through several countries, and many of them still lack any treaty. International water law is the set of rules and agreements governing how states share transboundary waters: rivers, lakes, seas or groundwater bordered by two or more states. Countries negotiate such agreements to lower the risk of conflict, often focusing on infrastructure and water quality. The UNECE Water Convention, signed in Helsinki in 1992, entered into force on 6 October 1996. Some legal principles can backfire. "Prior appropriation" and "riparianism" can deepen conflict by fixing in law who has plenty of water and who has too little.

nature-gov-160.title: Where science meets policy
nature-gov-160.text: Scientists and politicians treat uncertainty very differently, which makes it hard to turn research into rules. The science-policy interface is the meeting ground where the two work together, so research can inform decisions and be guided by them. The IPCC was the first of three global panels built for this. A biodiversity panel followed in 2012, for biodiversity and ecosystem services, and a panel on chemicals, waste and pollution came in 2025. A review of pollution still found no globally backed formal interface to guide action, research and funding.

nature-gov-115.title: Collaborative environmental governance
nature-gov-115.text: Rivers, forests and fisheries rarely respect the lines between agencies and jurisdictions. Collaborative environmental governance builds cooperation among actors across those scales to manage linked human and natural systems. It can create new knowledge through social learning, where what individuals learn together changes a whole community's understanding. It can also bring Indigenous and traditional knowledge into decisions, which may raise trust and a sense of fairness. The costs are real. Collaboration takes time and resources and can be too slow for urgent problems. Where large state actors dominate, it can become co-optation that deepens uneven power.

nature-gov-157.title: Environmental policy beyond the nation
nature-gov-157.text: As of 2018, more than 1,800 multilateral environmental agreements were in effect, more than 190 of them on climate change. Transnational environmental policy tackles global problems such as climate change, ozone depletion and marine pollution, with actors from at least two sovereign states. The 1972 Stockholm conference is seen as the start of international environmental law and policy. Not all the action is government-led. Transnational NGOs push change through market-based certification, and the Forest Stewardship Council is among the most successful examples.

nature-gov-155.title: Transition management: steering toward sustainability
nature-gov-155.text: In the early 2000s the Dutch government tried to steer a radical transformation of its energy system. It used transition management, a way of speeding sustainability transitions through shared visions, learning and experiments. Participants meet in a "transition arena" to define common problems and goals. These ideas are then tested in small experiments and reflected on. The approach takes a long view of one to three generations and favors "learn by doing, doing by learning" at the level of small, innovative niches. It does not command change. It nudges and redirects actors' choices toward sustainability. With few case studies, its method is still debated.

nature-gov-156.title: Landscapes, regimes and niches: how systems change
nature-gov-156.text: Why do new technologies sometimes break through and sometimes stall? The multi-level perspective sees change in systems that combine technology and society as unfolding on three levels. The landscape is the wide setting of values, beliefs, institutions and market conditions, and it shifts slowly. The regime is the set of dominant practices, rules and technologies that keeps the current system stable. Niches are where innovations start. When the landscape shifts, as with rising environmental awareness, it pressures regimes such as aviation and agriculture. That opens room for new technologies from the niches.

reviews.environmental-governance: The chapter's big shift is from managing single resources to managing the people who use whole ecosystems, learning by monitoring as they go. Countries tie themselves together through treaties, from the 1857 Lake Constance deal to conventions on ozone, hazardous waste, air pollution and the sea, yet no country can be forced to join, and free riders weaken every deal. Power is spread across levels and centers, from the EU and UN bodies down to towns writing their own local plans and fishing communities sharing rules with government. Ostrom's work showed that communities can govern shared resources well, while critics warn that participation and collaboration can favor the already powerful. Courts, citizens' rights to information and new research on whole-planet governance all push in the same direction: people affected by environmental decisions want a say in them.
